3\. Mine ARI systems research innovations and applications
----------------------------------------------------------

The mining industry is advancing state-of-the-art technologies by adopting ARI systems to improve workplace safety and health, production efficiencies, and mine economics. Research is also advancing frontiers of ARI systems to create the basis of tomorrow's technologies. This paper reviews and highlights ARI research and applications, contributions, achievements, ARI frontiers, and the gaps requiring attention. An increasingly autonomous operation requires the use of perceptive systems, autonomous and multi-modal sensing technologies to collect and process data for intelligent information for making real-time decisions with little or no human interventions. Mine operating practices must be updated on the conditions of the excavation geometries or processes because automated and robotic technologies require high-quality information about their surroundings. Expert-level context regarding the mining environment can be obtained for modeling and automation using novel sensing technologies. The collected data is fused to yield higher-level information for use by humans and machines. The use of robust mining systems with the ability to track the current state of operating entities within the system boundaries is required for making optimized control decisions. High-tech mines are increasingly deploying intelligent platforms and data analytics for achieving workplace safety and health, efficiency, and economic objectives.

### 3.1. Applications and frontiers of intelligent prospecting and exploration

[Mineral exploration](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/mineral-exploration "Learn more about Mineral exploration from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") focuses on the discovery and evaluation of potential [mineral deposits](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/mineral-deposit "Learn more about mineral deposits from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") using geological, geophysical, and metallurgical methods after the initial prospecting to define potential acreages. These methods culminate in defining anomalies for drilling, sampling, and assaying to determine the quantity and quality of deposits \[[2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib2)\]. Mineral prospecting is often carried out using direct visual examination, geophysical, [geochemistry](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geochemistry "Learn more about geochemistry from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), and [geobotany](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geobotany "Learn more about geobotany from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") techniques. The mining industry is increasingly deploying autonomous robots, [unmanned aerial vehicles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/pilotless-aircraft "Learn more about unmanned aerial vehicles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (UAVs), and drones for prospecting and exploration. This new paradigm uses [remote sensing](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/remote-sensing "Learn more about remote sensing from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), data analytics, 3D mapping and modelling, along with automated systems for maintenance, sorting, and processing \[[3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib3)\]. The integration of AI in mining operations marks a notable trend focused on harnessing predictive analytics to boost operational efficiency \[[4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib4),[5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib5)\].

Applications of AI and ML in mineral exploration combines the use of drone technology with the use of sensors such as light detection and ranging (LiDAR) for detailed mapping of mining sites, including hard-to-reach areas. Exploration and prospecting require extensive data collection and analysis, traditionally involving significant human labor, site visits to remote areas, manual sampling, assaying, and the use of primitive techniques lasting anywhere from two to twenty years \[[6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib6)\]. Exploration typically begins with the examination of historical records, including old maps, mining reports, and local stories about mineral discoveries. Early prospectors conducted extensive on-foot surveys, visually inspecting the landscape to identify signs of mineralization, such as unusual rock formations or characteristics such as color, luster, looking for surface indications of minerals like outcrops or float rocks for initial [reconnaissance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/reconnaissance "Learn more about reconnaissance from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages").

Modern [remote sensing technologies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/remote-sensing-technology "Learn more about remote sensing technologies from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), such as drones and satellite imagery, offer high-resolution geological maps and data. Drones are particularly useful for observing, surveying and mapping mine environments, tracking mine activities, and detecting topographic changes in the mining area, providing valuable data that can be used to guide mine planning and ensure safety. An example is a novel map exploration strategy which has been conducted to detect frontier points in 3D map representations. This demonstrates efficient exploration with comparable performance to image processing-based techniques including multi-robot 3D exploration and exploration from various initiation points \[[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib7)\]. Leveraging drone technology helps mining operations gain real-time insights, leading to more efficient and safer practices \[[8](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib8)\]. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) facilitate the integration and analysis of spatial data, enhancing decision-making processes \[[9](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib9)\]. ML algorithms leverage historical data to predict potential mineralization zones more accurately and efficiently than traditional manual methods. AI algorithms are used to analyze large databases to predict the occurrence of valuable minerals \[[10](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib10)\]. Software systems such as VRIFY AI and Geosoft's Oasis montaj can autonomously analyze geological data and identify promising exploration targets, thereby reducing the time and effort required for manual surveys \[[11](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib11)\]. [Artificial neural networks](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/artificial-neural-network "Learn more about Artificial neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (ANNs) have been used in exploration and reserve estimation to define mineral deposits \[[12](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib12)\]. Typically, the input data consists of samples with known 3D spatial positions, and predictive analyses are conducted based on the relationship between the modeled parameters and the sample locations.

Several recent studies demonstrate the power of ML based fault detection and monitoring frameworks in industrial applications. For instance, Ali et al. \[[13](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib13)\] proposed a robust statistical fault detection model using distributed canonical correlation analysis and low frequency control charts, which achieved fault detection rates of 100% and a false alarm rate of only 0.2%. Building on this, Ali et al. presented a dynamic, explainable fusion monitoring system that employs Granger entropy, time delay graph structures, and Shannon information theory to identify root causes of anomalies, offering real time transparency in [fault propagation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/fault-propagation "Learn more about fault propagation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") \[[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib14)\]. Another framework introduced by the same authors integrates dynamic independent component analysis with canonical correlation analysis and statistical distribution tools, further enhancing explainability and reliability in monitoring multivariate systems \[[14](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib14)\]. Additionally, their work on monitoring physio chemical processes using hybrid ML techniques confirmed that combining real time analytics with causality modeling significantly improves response times in safety critical environments \[[15](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib15)\]. These models are especially relevant to the mining sector where data from [haulage](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/haulage "Learn more about haulage from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") systems, [drilling rigs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/drilling-rig "Learn more about drilling rigs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), or chemical processing units can be harnessed for predictive insights. Their integration supports early warning systems, adaptive control, and informed decision making which are cornerstones for achieving zero harm and maximum operational uptime.

A work on semi-supervised learning technique with a convolutional neural network (CNN) model which accurately delineates [geological features](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geological-feature "Learn more about geological features from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") from 3D [seismic data](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/seismic-data "Learn more about seismic data from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") was conducted. This study automates geological feature detection in 3D seismic data, enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and consistency \[[16](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib16)\]. Advanced digital terrain modeling delivers detailed topographical information, aiding in the selection of areas with a higher likelihood of containing mineral deposits. Field applications include detection and classification of terrain features for automated identification of [geomorphological features](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geomorphological-feature "Learn more about geomorphological features from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") utilizing faster recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) deep learning model with a Zeiler and Fergus network (ZF-Net) \[[17](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib17)\]. Automated geophysical instruments and drones, equipped with sensors, conduct comprehensive surveys, provide detailed subsurface data for target-oriented mapping system utilizing UAVs and deep neural networks to detect, localize, and map critical geologic parameters \[[18](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib18)\]. Automated geochemical equipment enhances the speed and accuracy of sample testing \[[8](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib8)\]. Automated and semi-automated drilling rigs improve the efficiency and safety of core drilling, ensuring consistent and precise sample collection. Robotics in sampling can perform tasks such as trenching and pitting with greater precision and less human labor, resulting in more accurate data collection. Automated laboratory equipment perform assays with increased accuracy and speed, reducing human error and processing times with X-ray fluorescence and mass spectrometry for detailed compositional analysis of samples, with precise assessments of mineral content \[[19](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib19)\]. Advanced software such as GOCAD® Mining Suite and K-MINE [Geology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geology "Learn more about Geology from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") Module generate detailed 3D models of mineral deposits, integrating various data sources to provide a comprehensive understanding of mineral deposits.

The Borden Gold Project in Ontario, Canada, operated by Goldcorp Inc. (now part of Newmont Corporation), leveraged AI and advanced [geophysical surveys](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geophysical-survey "Learn more about geophysical surveys from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") to revolutionize exploration efforts. By employing ML algorithms, the project identified high-potential gold deposits with increased accuracy, significantly reducing exploration time and costs. These innovations yielded a 20% reduction in exploration timelines and a 35% improvement in drilling success rates, demonstrating the potential of AI-driven tools in mineral exploration. This project demonstrates how technology integration enhances efficiency and decision-making in resource identification \[[20](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib20)\].

### 3.2. Intelligent technologies for drilling and blasting operations

ANNs are effective in addressing complex rock fragmentation and associated environmental hazards caused by blasting, offering higher prediction accuracy and robustness \[[21](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib21)\]. An ANN model was used in blast operations to reduce ground vibration and [air blast](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/aerial-explosion "Learn more about air blast from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") below threshold limits, improve rock fragmentation, and identify the most sensitive and influential parameters for optimizing blasting operations \[[22](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib22)\]. State-of-the-art drilling and blasting technologies such as BastIQ and WebGen by Orica, innovative blasting practices and evolution in drilling and blasting trends are presented. These technologies emphasize the need for adaptive blast designs based on rock mass properties, enabling improved performance, safety and continuous optimization through innovative practices and evolving techniques \[[23](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib23)\]. Automated technologies are used to navigate continuous miners in tight spaces for coal extraction without human intervention. The automated technologies boost drilling productivity and enable access to previously unreachable mineral seams. It also reduces human exposure to hazardous conditions, such as dust, noise, gas, water, moving equipment, and potential roof collapses, thus improving workplace safety and health \[[24](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib24)\]. Robotic explosive charging system \[[25](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib25)\] autonomously performs: (1) detects blast holes; (2) controls teleoperated arm pose; (3) controls automatic arm pose; and (4) reduces human intervention through visual servoing. The system uses a laser scanner to survey the drill holes locations and matches the surveyed data against a pre-loaded blast plan. It is equipped with a laser rangefinder to pinpoint the exact locations of blast holes, along with video cameras and LED lights to support both automatic and manual hose insertion. The blast hole locations are extracted and displayed through a human–machine interface, providing a clear pattern visualization.

Epiroc, in collaboration with Orica, has invented Avatel, an autonomous explosives charging system that deploys explosives and completes charging cycle safely. It has an onboard technology that allows an operator to safely prepare and charge a development face with explosives. The system was introduced at Newcrest's Cadia Underground Mine in 2022 as the first commercial trial in the world \[[26](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib26),[27](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib27)\]. The robotized drilling machine (RDM) is designed to enhance safety in underground mining, particularly in gassy coal mines, by automating the deep hole drilling process \[[28](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib28)\]. The RDM consists of two main components: A telecontrol station and a main control station. The telecontrol station allows operators to issue commands and monitor drilling activity from a safe distance via a liquid crystal display. The main control station executes these commands and adjusts the drilling force during operations. A TV system with a camera at the drilling site provides live footage to enhance operator awareness and safety. Additionally, a multi-modal sensor suite system monitors parameters, such as position, pressure, temperature, and gas levels to ensure safe and efficient operation.

ABB's Robot Charger \[[29](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib29)\], tested at Sweden's Boliden Garpenberg Mine, uses an integrated vision system to locate drilled holes on a rock face. It is fitted to a charging carrier vehicle, which enters the mine face and autonomously charges drilled holes with explosives via a detonator-equipped charging hose. The process is repeated hole by hole, enhancing safety, efficiency, and productivity in mining operations.

At the Aitik Copper Mine in Sweden, Boliden AB implemented [Global Positioning System](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/global-positioning-system "Learn more about Global Positioning System from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (GPS) controlled drilling systems and electronic blasting technologies to optimize drilling and blasting operations. These technologies enhanced fragmentation control, enabling smoother downstream mineral processing and reducing over-break and under-break during blasting. The project achieved a 25% increase in blasting efficiency and a 10% reduction in drilling and blasting costs per ton of ore. This precision-focused approach highlights the importance of advanced control systems in improving productivity and lowering operational costs in mining \[[30](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib30)\].

### 3.3. Intelligent source-destination materials supply chain

The load-haul materials supply chain ensures continuous materials supply from mining faces to [crushers](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/crusher "Learn more about crushers from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), stockpiles, or [waste dumps](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/waste-dump "Learn more about waste dumps from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Automating the loading and hauling process improves accuracy, reduces manual errors, and enhances productivity. The autonomous haul truck (AHT) is a mobile robot that operates in difficult, challenging, and dynamic environments, requiring a high degree of sensing and perception, situational awareness, localization, and control \[[31](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib31)\]. The AHT challenges \[[3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib3)\] include but not limited to: (i) constantly changing mining geometries limiting the ability to install fixed infrastructure; (ii) decreased [Global Navigation Satellite System](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/gnss "Learn more about Global Navigation Satellite System from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (GNSS) reliability due to restricted access; (iii) safety and integrity challenges due to the mix of manual and automated fleets of machines; and (iv) severe weather challenges. The AHT system constructs a virtual 3D configuration that is in sync with onboard technologies in excavators and dump trucks. Creating models that automatically develop a zoning strategy for rocks allows for more precise planning, design, and management of mining operations. Robotic excavators, which are part of a self-developing system for zoning rocks, can improve mining operations \[[32](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib32)\]. In most surface mines, dozers are essential and require operators with significant expertise in controlling ground-engaging tools and machine positioning. Operators face several health risks, including whole-body vibrations, awkward postures, and high noise levels. These factors can lead to health issues over time. The advent of robotic dozing has significantly improved safety and health conditions for personnel by reducing exposure to these risks while maintaining efficiency and high productivity \[[33](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib33)\].

[Geological modeling](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geological-modeling "Learn more about Geological modeling from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") often uses mesh surfaces to define various geological zones, like mineralized regions and waste areas. Definition errors can have serious effects on grade estimation and ore recovery. A new framework for surface warping offers a solution by automatically correcting boundary placements with new data \[[34](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib34)\]. Automating this process enables ongoing updates to [ore body](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/ore-body "Learn more about ore body from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") models, allowing for near-real-time decision-making. UAVs, equipped with various sensors, are used in a variety of tasks, including 3D mapping, ore control, mapping of rock discontinuities, post-blast rock fragmentation measurement, and monitoring tailing stability. Rio Tinto and Komatsu have made significant progress in automating an [iron ore](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/iron-ore "Learn more about iron ore from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") quarry in the Pilbara region of Western Australia with the Komatsu 930E-4AT robotic mining trucks. These trucks are equipped with cameras, radars, and laser rangefinders for detection, tracking, perception, and for making real-time intelligent decisions. These sensors work with GPS navigation and [wireless communication](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/wireless-communication "Learn more about wireless communication from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") systems to navigate the mining site. An artificial intelligence system called FrontRunner creates a virtual 3D map of the terrain for the truck to understand its environment and plan its movements accordingly \[[35](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib35)\]. The AHT system has an obstacle detection system, allowing them to identify and avoid obstacles in their path, making them safer and more efficient during operation.

Fully autonomous trains transport iron ore from the mines to ports across the Pilbara region, which is a major advancement in the field of automated haulage. These technological innovations demonstrate the industry's growing reliance on automation, which has resulted in notable improvements in efficiency and safety. The AutoHaul technology, pioneered by Rio Tinto in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, is recognized as the world's first fully automated heavy-haul rail system. The system is designed to operate across more than 1866 ​km of track, allowing 220 trains to transport iron ore from 16 mines to four port terminals, and monitored remotely from a control station in Perth \[[36](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib36),[37](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib37)\]. AutoHaul represents a new paradigm shift in rail automation. It reduces downtime by eliminating the need for driver shift changes, improving operational efficiency. This technology also reduces road transportation, crew changes, emissions and fuel consumption by using hybrid power technology, with lithium-ion batteries to store energy generated during braking. Rio Tinto is also exploring [collision avoidance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/collision-avoidance "Learn more about collision avoidance from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") technology to improve safety by detecting and avoiding obstacles on the track \[[38](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib38)\].

The Jimblebar Iron Ore Mine in Pilbara, Western Australia, operated by Broken Hill Proprietary Group, achieved remarkable efficiency improvements through the deployment of an autonomous haulage system (AHS). By utilizing driverless trucks, the site optimized material movement, reduced human error, and operated continuously without delays associated with shift changes. As a result, material hauled per hour increased by 30%, operating costs decreased by 20%, and maintenance costs dropped by 50%. This transformation underscores the potential of autonomous technology to enhance safety and productivity in large-scale mining operations \[[39](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib39)\].

### 3.4. ARI technologies in mineral processing

Ore processing involves a series of methods to improve ore quality, beginning with comminution (crushing and grinding) and followed by screening, classification, and separation techniques \[[40](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib40)\]. ARI systems and technologies are applied across several domains in mineral processing, improving safety, health, and productivity while reducing operational costs. Automated systems have revolutionized the operation of crushers and mills by controlling feeding and processes, thereby boosting efficiency, and reducing manual labor. Sensors and real-time data analytics optimize grinding by monitoring machine health, ore characteristics, and operational parameters \[[41](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib41)\]. Modern flotation cells, equipped with automated control systems, adjust parameters like air flow and reagent addition in real-time for optimal performance \[[42](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib42)\]. Enhanced recovery rates and efficiency in [concentration processes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/concentration-process "Learn more about concentration processes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are achieved with advanced flotation cells, magnetic, and gravity separators. Intelligent control systems manage thickening and filtration, improving [water recovery](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/water-reclamation "Learn more about water recovery from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and minimizing manual intervention. Robotics and automation in smelting control temperatures, feed rates, and electrolysis conditions, ensuring consistent metal quality and energy efficiency.

Advanced process control systems analyze real-time data to optimize smelting and refining processes. Automated monitoring of [tailings dams](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/tailings-dam "Learn more about tailings dams from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and ponds enhances stability and prevents environmental contamination. Intelligent systems predict equipment failures and schedule maintenance, reducing downtime and improving plant availability. Modern tailings management employs [geotextiles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geotextile "Learn more about geotextiles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), paste backfill, dray stacking and advanced [dam construction](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/dam-construction "Learn more about dam construction from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") techniques to minimize environmental impacts \[[43](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib43)\]. Automation reduces variability, increases throughput, and optimizes resource utilization. Robotics and remote operations enhance safety by reducing human exposure to hazards. Intelligent systems manage emissions, reduce waste, and optimize resource recovery, leading to more sustainable operations. Automation and distributed control systems offer a balance of decentralized and centralized management, maintaining stable production quality \[[44](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib44)\]. Advanced analytical instruments enable precise monitoring and control. Robotics enhances safety through automated material handling and inspection tasks. Intelligent control systems, together with multivariate statistical process monitoring, manage complex processes with the ability to adapt to dynamic conditions.

Rio Tinto's Kennecott Utah Copper operation in the United States utilized real-time sensor data and advanced process control systems to enhance flotation efficiency. These innovations enabled a 10% improvement in copper recovery rates, an 8% reduction in energy consumption per ton of ore processed, and a 12% increase in reagent efficiency. The integration of predictive algorithms and real-time monitoring not only optimized mineral recovery but also significantly reduced processing costs, showcasing the value of data-driven approaches in mineral processing \[[45](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib45)\]. At the Sishen Iron Ore Mine in [South Africa](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/republic-of-south-africa "Learn more about South Africa from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), Kumba Iron Ore Limited, a subsidiary of Anglo-American plc, implemented an integrated operations center to centralize data from various mining processes. By leveraging real-time analytics and streamlined workflows, the mine improved decision-making across the value chain, from extraction to processing. These efforts resulted in a 20% improvement in operational efficiency, a 15% reduction in equipment downtime, and a 10% decrease in overall operational costs. This example highlights the benefits of end-to-end integration for achieving operational excellence and [sustainability](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/environmental-impact-assessment "Learn more about sustainability from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in mining.

4\. Robotics in mine rescue
---------------------------

Despite the rapid growth mine rescue technologies, miner safety remains a significant concern. Compared to other industries, mining and its related sectors have higher rates of workplace injuries and fatalities. Mining layout geometries are constantly changing with uncertainties, hazards, and dangerous operations. This dynamic environment makes mining akin to a battle against unpredictable natural forces, resulting in high rates of accidents, injuries, and illnesses. Thus, it is critical for the mining industry to continuously and meticulously identify potential hazards, evaluate the associated risks, and work continuously to reduce those risks to acceptable levels \[[46](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib46)\]. Certain cutting-edge technologies that provide intelligent responses and mine rescue challenges play a crucial role in decreasing mining-related fatalities and accidents. This section provides highlights on mine disasters, mine fatalities and how automation, AI, ML and robotics are being applied to improve mine rescue operations using robots.

### 4.1. Intelligent mine disaster and post-disaster management

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) classifies disasters by the number of fatalities and cause. MSHA defines a “disaster” as an incident with five or more fatalities. Mine disasters have long been a central concern for mine operators, safety and health personnel, miners, and mine safety and health researchers around the globe \[[47](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib47)\]. Since 1900, there have been hundreds of mine disasters that have led to thousands of miner fatalities \[[48](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib48)\]. The causes of mine disasters are classified into six categories \[[49](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib49)\] including: (1) explosions; (2) fires; (3) haulage accidents; (4) ground falls or bumps due to roof collapse of sudden forceful pillar burst; (5) inundations from water or toxic gases; and (6) other causes. Disaster management in mines can be either proactive or reactive. Proactive management involves taking steps to prevent and eliminate disasters through quick actions by operational and emergency staff. Reactive management, on the other hand, includes measures to reduce disaster impact, alleviate suffering, initiate recovery efforts, organize rehabilitation, and provide timely updates to victims' relatives, civil authorities, and the media. Tools such as GIS, [GPS](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/global-positioning-system "Learn more about GPS from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), Remote Sensing, Satellite Communication, and Modeling & Simulation techniques aid in identifying infrastructure, risk areas, and disaster zones, as well as in planning and implementing hazard reduction strategies \[[50](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib50)\].

### 4.2. Mine rescue robots

The initial hours following a mine disaster are critical in determining the survival of trapped miners \[[51](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib51)\]. During this time, deploying a wireless robot equipped with gas sensors and cameras that can operate in extremely low-light conditions could be crucial. Underground work faces challenges, such as confined spaces, high heat and humidity, unpleasant atmospheres, and poor lighting. After a disaster, these conditions worsen, making it difficult for rescue teams to access the affected areas in time. Due to the high levels of dust and smoke that fill the air, rescue teams often struggle to move forward, as they are blinded by the thick cloud of dust. This situation halts rescue operations, leading to the loss of precious hours. In coal mines, the situation is even more hazardous because of the presence of toxic and explosive gases and the risk of secondary explosions due to methane gas, coal dust or firedamp. In these scenarios, mobile subterranean robots are invaluable. These robots can be deployed immediately after an accident, regardless of the atmospheric conditions. Additionally, robots can be used for 3D mapping of the mine to collect critical data from hard-to-reach locations. Mine rescue robots are designed to enter mines during emergencies, find possible escape routes for those trapped, and assess whether it is safe for human entry. Localization is a key challenge in this context \[[50](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib50)\]. Four primary types of rescue robots are identified \[[52](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib52)\].

*   (1)[Unmanned ground vehicles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/unmanned-ground-vehicles "Learn more about Unmanned ground vehicles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (UGVs): These robots operate on land and are useful for rescuers in locating and interacting with trapped victims in areas that may be too risky or inaccessible for human rescue teams.
    
*   (2)Unmanned [surface vehicles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/surface-vehicle "Learn more about surface vehicles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (USVs): These robots are designed to operate on the surface of water. They assist rescuers by helping to identify victims and transporting necessary equipment to them.
    
*   (3)Unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs): These robots can search [underwater environments](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/underwater-environment "Learn more about underwater environments from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") to locate fatalities, hazardous materials, or other potential risks.
    
*   (4)[Unmanned aerial vehicles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/pilotless-aircraft "Learn more about Unmanned aerial vehicles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (UAVs): UAVs, or drones, can fly over the site without touching the ground, providing a broader view of the accident scene and delivering medical supplies to victims. They also offer rescuers an aerial perspective of disasters or accidents, aiding in assessment and planning.
    

A robot designed for underground rescue operations in high-risk mines should encompass attributes from all four types to effectively address the range of scenarios that may arise. These rescue robots include:

**i. Wolverine robot**

The Wolverine robot ([Fig. 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#fig2)), initially developed for military use, has been adapted for mining operations. Originally designed by Remotec, this robot was acquired in 2001 to function as a traditional bomb squad robot but has since been modified for mining applications. The Wolverine robot is remotely controlled through a fiber optic tether, allowing for safe operation from a distance of up to 152,400 ​cm. It is equipped with three cameras, providing live video feed to the operator for real-time monitoring, along with a gas sensor for continuous sampling \[[53](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib53)\]. This allows the operator to navigate and assess conditions remotely, reducing the risks involved in mine rescue operations. The Wolverine robot, despite its capabilities, had limitations due to its heavy weight and reliance on a fiber optic cable for communication. These factors affected its performance during certain mine disasters, preventing it from fulfilling its intended role. Although the robot was deployed in real-life mine rescue scenarios, it was unsuccessful in some instances, which has prompted Remotec to work on improving the design and functionality to overcome these challenges.

This capability enhances situational awareness and helps assess risks before human personnel enter dangerous zones. The robot's versatility also allows it to be adapted for other tasks, such as inspection, surveillance or exploration.

#### 4.2.1. Requirements of a rescue robot

Key design requirements for any rescue robot is that it must be intrinsically safe and flame-proof. Essential functions for rescue equipment include searching, inspection, and mapping. Other critical tasks are dirt removal, structural inspection, medical assistance, and casualty evacuation. Additionally, these robots can act as mobile repeaters, offer logistical support, and even serve as a substitute for a team member. Rescue robots should be equipped with various sensors for gas and temperature monitoring to ensure constant assessment of the environment, enabling rescue personnel to make quicker and more informed decisions \[[59](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib59)\]. All sensors and cameras must be durable, dustproof, waterproof, and of industrial-grade quality to withstand the harsh conditions typically found in underground mines. An intelligent response and rescue system for the mining industry must outline critical technologies such as underground positioning techniques and 3D modeling algorithms with four key components: A database, a monitoring center, a fixed underground sensor network, and mobile devices \[[60](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib60)\]. The database and sensor network provide real-time data on ground plants, underground facilities, environmental conditions, and miners' locations, supporting communication between the surface and underground sections. The monitoring center collects and relays this data to rescuers and decision-makers while mobile devices help underground personnel receive information, track positions, and communicate with the center \[[61](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib61)\].

5\. Economics of automation and robotic systems in mining
---------------------------------------------------------

As the mining industry confronts rising operational costs, [ore grade](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/ore-grade "Learn more about ore grade from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") depletion, and commodity market volatility, automation and robotics are emerging as key economic enablers. These technologies go beyond technical and safety improvements to deliver measurable cost savings, greater process efficiency, and enhanced long-term sustainability. This section examines the economic rationale for adopting automated and robotic systems in mining, focusing on cost-benefit dynamics, [return on investment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/return-on-investment "Learn more about return on investment from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (ROI), and their broader impact on mining-dependent communities. The economic viability of mining modernization increasingly depends on technological innovation in response to declining labor productivity and tightening environmental regulations. Zhironkin and Szurgacz \[[62](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib62)\] note that the combination of rising capital expenditures and depleting ore grades is compressing profit margins. Consequently, mining enterprises are investing in high-capacity, automated, and digitized systems to boost productivity and ensure investor confidence. Technologies such as [unmanned vehicles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/unmanned-vehicle "Learn more about unmanned vehicles from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), digital mine planning, and integrated geophysical surveying reduce energy use, prevent equipment failure, and streamline resource extraction. The adoption of Industry 4.0 tools, including AI and predictive analytics, enhances operational agility under market uncertainty.

Automation in mining represents a capital-deepening shift that reduces reliance on manual labor while supporting continuous operations \[[63](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib63)\]. This transformation lowers labor expenses and reduces exposure to safety hazards. However, the shift also brings consequences for local economies that historically relied on employment from mining. Declining job availability, reduced household incomes, and a shrinking tax base affect the socio-economic fabric of mining regions. While automation enhances feasibility for remote and high-risk operations, it also challenges the traditional rationale for public investment based on employment creation. Konyukh \[[64](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib64)\] introduces an economic evaluation framework that contrasts robotics with conventional mechanization. It accounts for initial capital costs, labor savings, and reductions in auxiliary expenses like ventilation and downtime. The model reveals that when more than five distinct manual tasks are automated, multifunctional robots become economically advantageous due to lower programming and design costs. Additionally, indirect labor-related costs such as training, health risks, and inconsistent human performance are estimated to range from 1.2 to 1.4 times the average wage. The framework includes a profitability index (_S_), which suggests robotic systems are justified when _S_ is greater than 1, indicating the benefits outweigh costs over the system's operational life.

Robotic Autonomous Mining Systems also drive economic gains by improving operational accuracy and asset utilization. Solutions such as Komatsu's Komtrax and Epiroc's Scooptram Automation Total have demonstrated their ability to cut fuel consumption, enable predictive maintenance, and optimize workflow. Battery-electric vehicles from Caterpillar and Komatsu offer additional savings by reducing energy needs and [ventilation requirements](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/ventilation-requirement "Learn more about ventilation requirements from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in underground mines \[[65](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib65)\]. Across the sector, automation reduces production costs by extending equipment life, minimizing wear, and limiting idle time. Comparisons with port automation indicate that autonomous systems can lower operating expenses by up to 30%, primarily through more efficient fuel use and reduced shift-related downtime. Despite these long-term benefits, high capital investment and system integration complexity remain significant adoption barriers \[[66](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib66)\]. Achieving economic potential from automation also requires data intelligence. Predictive analytics, real-time monitoring, and adaptive mine planning tools allow companies to anticipate failures, adjust machine behavior, and enhance scheduling accuracy. These technologies, when integrated with AI-driven systems, help minimize uncertainty and improve resource utilization across the value chain \[[67](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib67)\].

Lopes et al. \[[68](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib68)\] emphasize that robotics enhance productivity not by increasing extraction rates, but by maintaining consistent output and reducing operational pauses. Autonomous load-haul-dump units can save up to 2–3 ​h per shift and improve output by approximately 20%. Eliminating human-related factors such as fatigue and error leads to fewer disruptions, lower insurance liabilities, and reduced health-related costs. However, the need for skilled personnel in maintenance and troubleshooting persists, and initial implementation costs remain high. AI-driven automation also strengthens profitability through more accurate [ore body](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/ore-body "Learn more about ore body from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") modeling, optimized equipment management, and reduced waste \[[69](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib69)\]. These capabilities improve output per unit input, increasing operational resilience during commodity downturns. Over time, the combination of data-informed decisions and performance optimization contributes to sustainable economic performance. Yoshida \[[70](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib70)\] highlights that despite its potential to reduce workplace injuries, the adoption of robotics in high-risk industries like mining often lags due to profit-driven priorities. Investment is more common in high-margin sectors like automotive and warehousing. In mining, although robots can lower injury rates and increase reliability, decisions to automate are frequently motivated more by labor cost savings than long-term safety benefits.

The socioeconomic implications of mining automation are multifaceted. While it displaces some traditional roles, it creates demand for highly skilled labor in robotics, AI, and systems integration. This transition requires companies to invest in workforce reskilling and training. At the same time, reduced employment and wage-based tax revenues challenge the fiscal stability of mining communities. As noted by Kojas et al. \[[71](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib71)\], addressing these disparities will require compensation mechanisms such as regional revenue-sharing and public investment in human capital development to ensure that automation contributes to inclusive economic growth. In summary, automation and robotics offer compelling economic advantages in mining through labor efficiency gains, cost reduction, and operational optimization \[[72](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib72)\]. Yet, realizing their full value demands strategic planning that balances profitability with social responsibility. Mining enterprises must align technology integration with broader development goals, including reskilling initiatives and equitable investment strategies, to ensure sustainable, long-term economic outcomes for both industry and community stakeholders. Strategic partnerships between industry and government will be critical to ensure these transitions deliver both economic and social value. 6\. Barriers in automation – Challenges and limitations of ARI systems in mining
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Although ARI systems offer substantial economic and operational benefits as well as improved safety for the mining industry, their widespread adoption is hindered by a range of technical, regulatory, social, organizational, and infrastructural challenges. These barriers impact not only the pace of technology deployment but also limit the scalability, interoperability, and long-term integration of ARI systems across diverse mining environments. A key social challenge is the erosion of the social license to operate, particularly in areas where employment generation is a central expectation of mining investments. Projects that fail to deliver anticipated job creation often face resistance from communities and political stakeholders \[[63](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib63)\]. This issue is compounded by the lack of skilled labor in remote mining regions, where the advanced technical expertise required to operate ARI systems is more readily available in urban centers. In addition, the scarcity of reliable employment data, especially regarding subcontracted workers, limits the ability of policymakers to evaluate the full socioeconomic impacts of automation and develop targeted responses.

Technical challenges further complicate ARI system integration. In underground load-haul-dump operations, visibility coefficients ranging from 0.4 to 0.6, combined with dust, poor lighting, and confined spaces, reduce the effectiveness of remote and robotic control \[[64](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib64)\]. These harsh conditions limit the operational capability of robotic systems, which often lack the dexterity and adaptability needed for tasks such as blasting, assembly, or [autonomous navigation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/autonomous-navigation "Learn more about autonomous navigation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in complex geological environments. Communication reliability poses another major barrier. Geological obstructions in underground mines often interfere with signal transmission, making real-time remote control unreliable. Current reliance on Wi-Fi and 4G networks is frequently inadequate for supporting continuous data flow in deep or geologically complex areas \[[65](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib65)\]. Additionally, the absence of unified standards for perception, decision-making algorithms, and control architectures results in inconsistent system performance. This lack of standardization across original equipment manufacturers creates isolated systems that cannot communicate or share data efficiently, thus fragmenting operations and increasing maintenance burdens \[[66](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib66)\]. Legacy infrastructure presents a substantial barrier to the deployment of intelligent systems. Many mines continue to operate using outdated, fragmented platforms that are incompatible with modern digital technologies. Integrating ARI systems into these environments requires foundational upgrades, which are both capital-intensive and logistically complex. Without such modernization, the full benefits of automation cannot be realized. One of the most persistent technical challenges is the integration of AI with legacy systems, which often leads to performance bottlenecks, system incompatibility, and inefficient workflows \[[62](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib62),[73](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib73)\].

Human-system integration remains a significant concern. Mining environments are inherently unpredictable, requiring human intervention when automated systems encounter dynamic or unforeseen scenarios. Failures stemming from brittle automation logic, misconfigured task execution, or inconsistent behavior in changing conditions introduce safety risks that current technologies are not fully equipped to manage. In many developing countries, political and social resistance to ARI systems is also intensified by fears of job displacement and a lack of effective stakeholder engagement \[[67](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib67)\]. Cost remains a major constraint to ARI adoption. Small and medium-sized mining enterprises often lack the financial resources to absorb the high capital expenditures required for implementation. These costs include not only the purchase of ARI systems but also the modernization of supporting infrastructure and workforce training. Furthermore, the safety-critical nature of mining operations necessitates rigorous testing, verification, and regulatory approval of ARI technologies, which extends deployment timelines and increases operational costs \[[67](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib67)\]. Legal, ethical, and regulatory uncertainties further restrict adoption. The absence of comprehensive laws governing liability, decision attribution, and data privacy in autonomous operations creates significant compliance risks. Ethical challenges emerge particularly in situations where ARI systems operate in hazardous environments with minimal human supervision, and where errors or accidents could occur without clear accountability \[[68](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib68)\]. Societal and labor market dynamics further influence ARI adoption. In regions where low-cost labor is abundant, investment in automation is often deprioritized. Yoshida \[[70](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib70)\] identifies this availability of inexpensive human labor as a structural barrier that discourages the adoption of capital-intensive intelligent systems. Moreover, underreporting of workplace injuries distorts safety statistics and reduces pressure on companies to automate high–risk activities.

Another significant limitation lies in data quality and availability. AI and ML models in mining require access to large volumes of high-quality, structured data. However, [mining data](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/data-mining "Learn more about mining data from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is frequently fragmented, inconsistent, or biased, leading to unreliable predictions and poor generalization in tasks such as [rock fracture](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/rock-fracture "Learn more about rock fracture from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") prediction and force-controlled drilling. In many cases, limitations in sensor integration and inconsistencies in data acquisition reduce the reliability of analytics outputs. Organizational resistance to change, coupled with a shortage of skilled professionals capable of implementing and maintaining these systems, also impedes technological advancement \[[69](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib69)\]. The complexity of integrating advanced systems such as fleet management platforms into mining operations highlights several additional barriers. The use of [telematics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/telematics "Learn more about telematics from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), GPS, IoT sensors, and analytics tools across different types of equipment and manufacturers often leads to compatibility issues. Connectivity remains a persistent concern in remote and underground locations, limiting the real-time responsiveness of such systems. Additionally, the volume of data generated can lead to overload if robust analytics tools and trained personnel are not in place to interpret the information for decision-making. Resistance to change and limited digital literacy among workers further complicate implementation, necessitating comprehensive training and change management strategies \[[74](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib74)\]. DT technologies and their enabling systems also face multiple technical and organizational challenges. For instance, a single autonomous haul truck can generate up to 2.5 terabytes of sensor data per day, most of which remains underutilized due to limitations in processing, storage, and [data fusion](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/multisensor-fusion "Learn more about data fusion from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") capabilities. In underground operations, the harsh environmental conditions and connectivity issues further hinder the deployment of real-time DT. Organizationally, many companies lack cohesion between their information technology and operations teams, resulting in fragmented deployments and poor scalability. Furthermore, digital transformation efforts are often viewed as marginal IT projects rather than as central to strategic business goals. The lack of standardized frameworks, inadequate cybersecurity practices, and limited infrastructure, particularly in developing regions, continue to slow the adoption of intelligent, data-driven mining systems \[[75](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib75)\].

Several critical technological gaps persist in the global mining sector. Emere et al. \[[76](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib76)\] highlight that while progress has been made in adopting AI, IoT, and blockchain technologies, limited attention has been paid to other transformative innovations such as 3D printing, augmented reality, and virtual reality. These technologies could significantly enhance equipment maintenance, training, and operational safety, yet remain underutilized. The principles of Industry 4.0, which include the convergence of cyber-physical systems, [big data analytics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/big-data-analytics "Learn more about big data analytics from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), AI, and IoT, have gained traction in large-scale industrial applications. Industry 4.0 as a paradigm shift from traditional industrial models to highly interconnected and autonomous production systems. However, the adoption of these principles within the mining sector, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises, remains limited due to several barriers. These include high initial investment costs, outdated infrastructure, limited interoperability, insufficient awareness among decision-makers, and growing cybersecurity concerns. Ingaldi and Ulewicz \[[77](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib77)\] argue that the lack of digital skills and organizational readiness further complicates implementation, and that continuous training and policy support are essential for sustainable digital transformation.

Barriers to automation are not confined to mining alone. Insights from the public sector, particularly in the adoption of Robotic Process Automation, reveal parallel issues. Many government processes are legally constrained, highly variable, and difficult to standardize for automation. Challenges also include fragmented IT systems, organizational resistance, and low digital readiness among staff and citizens. In some cases, automated systems may exclude vulnerable populations such as non-native language speakers, illustrating the need for tailored and inclusive design approaches. These cross-sectoral challenges reinforce the argument that automation requires thoughtful, context-specific planning and strong stakeholder alignment. In conclusion, the deployment of ARI systems in mining is obstructed by the convergence of technical limitations, infrastructure inadequacies, uncertain regulatory environments, high investment demands, limited labor capacity, and sociopolitical resistance. Overcoming these barriers will require coordinated action in the form of regulatory reform, strategic workforce development, infrastructure modernization, system interoperability, and inclusive innovation strategies. Without these critical enablers, the transformative potential of intelligent systems in mining will remain unrealized \[[71](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib71)\].

7\. Roadmap for deployment of ARI
---------------------------------

The trajectory toward full deployment maturity of ARI systems in the mining industry follows a phased evolution. These phases include research and prototyping (2020–2025), early adoption and testing (2024–2028), scaled commercialization (2027–2032), and full integration maturity (2030–2045). Several systems have progressed into advanced stages, while others remain in pilot or conceptual development. The roadmap's success depends on both technological innovation and readiness factors such as regulation, skilled labor availability, and infrastructure. AHS are currently the most mature ARI application \[[78](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib78)\]. With established deployments in Australia and North America, companies such as Komatsu and Caterpillar have achieved operational success with their FrontRunner and MineStar Command systems \[[79](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib79)\]. These are projected to reach global maturity between 2027 and 2032 as terrain-adaptive capabilities, fifth-generation communications, and safety protocols are further refined \[[80](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib80),[81](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib81)\]. Drill automation and blast optimization technologies led by providers including Epiroc and Sandvik are expected to reach maturity by 2030, with integration into digital mine planning and real-time feedback loops becoming standard \[[81](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib81)\].

AI-driven predictive maintenance systems are likely to be fully adopted between 2026 and 2028, enabled by the widespread use of sensors, edge computing, and artificial intelligence models that detect equipment anomalies before failure occurs \[[80](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib80)\]. Robotic inspection tools such as drones, crawler bots, and remote visual inspection units have already gained momentum, with deployment maturity expected between 2025 and 2027, particularly in hazardous environments and hard-to-reach mining zones \[[82](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib82)\]. Similarly, safety analytics powered by AI including fatigue monitoring, proximity detection, and [collision avoidance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/collision-avoidance "Learn more about collision avoidance from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are on track to achieve widespread implementation between 2028 and 2035, although regulatory compliance and integration with legacy systems remain challenges \[[83](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib83)\]. Fully autonomous mine ecosystems characterized by real-time DT, centralized AI platforms, and end-to-end automated workflows are anticipated to reach maturity between 2035 and 2045. Achieving this vision depends significantly on interoperability among equipment manufacturers, digital infrastructure in remote locations, cybersecurity safeguards, and AI governance protocols \[[84](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib84),[81](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib81)\].

Timelines will be influenced by both enabling and limiting factors. Accelerators include increasing environmental, social, and governance standards, regulatory safety mandates, and demonstrated operational [return on investment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/return-on-investment "Learn more about return on investment from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). However, challenges such as high capital investment, workforce reskilling gaps, fragmented data systems, and community resistance in employment-sensitive regions may delay adoption \[[80](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib80),[81](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib81),[84](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949926725000320#bib84)\].

If current innovation trends and investment levels are maintained, the mining industry can expect to achieve full operational maturity of key ARI systems by the mid-2030s. Widespread adoption of fully autonomous and interoperable digital mines, particularly in developing regions, may extend into the 2040s.
